title: Photon-mediated thermodynamics and density fluctuations in an ensemble of laser-cooled Cesium atoms
authors: Arnab Ghosh, Inderpreet Kaur, Hemant Yadav, Shiva Kant Dwivedi, R Shanmukesh, Mithun Thudiyangal, Matthew J. Davis, Bodhaditya Santra
abstract: We present an experimental study of detuning-dependent properties of a laser-cooled cesium cloud in a magneto-optical trap. Fluorescence images are used to extract the cloud size, shot-to-shot width fluctuations, optical depth, density profiles, and spatial density fluctuation spectra as the trapping-laser detuning is varied. Near resonance, the cloud exhibits larger spatial extent, increased width fluctuations, higher optical depth, and enhanced density-fluctuation power, while larger detunings produce a more reproducible and spatially confined cloud. The measured density profiles are analysed phenomenologically using a generalized Lane-Emden model with a polytropic equation of state, yielding detuning-dependent effective fit parameters in a weak-interaction regime. Power-spectrum and autocorrelation analyses reveal reproducible scale-dependent density correlations. The results provide a quantitative characterization of detuning-dependent radiative and collective effects in a cesium MOT and establish a basis for future measurements that can more directly test nonequilibrium transport and photon-mediated interaction models.
summary: This study experimentally investigates how varying the laser detuning affects the collective behavior of laser-cooled Cesium atoms in a MOT. By measuring cloud size, density fluctuations, and analyzing the data with a Lane-Emden model, the authors show that strong photon-mediated interactions are enhanced near resonance, leading to increased density fluctuations and a deviation from simple ideal gas behavior.
main_problem: To experimentally characterize detuning-dependent radiative and collective effects in a laser-cooled Cesium Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) and establish a basis for testing nonequilibrium transport and photon-mediated interaction models.
main_result: The cloud size, density fluctuations, and mean vibrational occupation number are strongly dependent on the laser detuning, showing enhanced fluctuations and density near resonance due to increased photon scattering.
method: Fluorescence imaging and power-spectrum analysis are used to measure cloud size, density profiles, and spatial density fluctuation spectra as the trapping-laser detuning is varied.
model_or_system: The system is a cloud of laser-cooled Cesium atoms confined in a MOT. Analysis involves fitting density profiles to a generalized Lane-Emden model, which describes the density distribution under the influence of trapping and multiple-scattering forces.
key_observables: Cloud size/width fluctuations, optical depth, density profiles, spatial density-fluctuation spectra, mean vibrational occupation number ($ ar{n}$), and effective polytropic parameters ($\gamma, \Omega$).
important_parameters: Laser detuning ($\delta$), trapping laser power (7 mW), and the ratio of scattering rates near resonance vs. far detuning.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a phenomenological generalized Lane-Emden model and does not assume the system is in global thermodynamic equilibrium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, timing sequence, histograms of cloud-width fluctuations vs. detuning, and plots showing the dependence of $ ar{n}$, optical depth, and model parameters ($\gamma, \Omega$) on detuning.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from describing the experimental setup and measurements (varying detuning) to analyzing global observables (width fluctuations, optical depth) and finally applying theoretical modeling (Lane-Emden equation) to characterize the underlying collective radiative effects.
why_interesting: This work provides quantitative experimental data linking the detuning of the trapping laser to measurable collective effects like density fluctuations and effective equation of state parameters, offering a platform to test non-equilibrium transport models in ultracold atomic gases.
